title: Rebbe Nachman's circle of joy
hookLine: Rebbe Nachman taught that being joyful always is a great mitzvah
carry: joy is a mitzvah, kept up on hard days
tomorrow: If you can damage, you can repair
last: TWO SOULS, ONE CITY: LET THE GODLY SOUL LEAD.

lines: A MAN WITH A HEAVY FACE.
cards: A wedding, late at night. The music is loud and a circle of dancers is spinning. Off to the side stands a man who isn't dancing.
His face is heavy. Something is wrong in his life, and it shows. Then two of the dancers break the circle, take him by the hands, and pull him in.
He resists for a step or two. Then he's turning with them, still carrying whatever he carries, but carried along too. Rebbe Nachman of Breslov used a scene like this to teach about joy.
And he made a demand about it that sounds impossible.

teach.b: Always joyful. Rebbe Nachman taught that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always. First, the word always.

In Hebrew it's tamid, the word for the offering that was brought in the Temple without a break, morning and evening. The psalm uses it too: "I have set the LORD always before me." Always isn't a mood.
It's a practice that keeps going.
Second, it's work. Rebbe Nachman didn't pretend joy comes easily.

Breslov teaching passes on his advice that a person should push with all their strength to be glad, and when nothing else works, to do something a little silly, something light, to break the heaviness.
Joy, here, is something you make, not something you wait for. Third, the circle. That's the scene from the hook, and it's his.
When joy is strong, it doesn't run from sadness.

teach.h: JOY PULLS SADNESS INTO THE DANCE.
teach.b: It reaches over, takes sadness by the hands, and pulls it into the dance. The sadness isn't erased. It's brought in, and it starts to move.
Fourth, how this differs from a week ago. Simcha, a week ago, opened the heart. Rebbe Nachman adds the hard part: always.
Especially then. Not because pain doesn't matter, but because, for him, a heavy heart is the very place joy is needed most.

how: Breslov Hasidim sing and dance as a deliberate practice of joy, and the saying that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always has been set to song.

o: joy as a steady practice, kept up even on hard days
a promise that faithful people never feel sad
a festival of dancing held once a year

p: I have set the LORD always before me
a great mitzvah to be joyful always

s: Rebbe Nachman taught that joy comes easily
he taught that a person should push for joy with all their strength.
in his image, joy pulls sadness into the dance
sadness isn't erased. it's brought into the circle, and starts to move.
always joyful means pain doesn't matter
for him, a heavy heart is the very place joy is needed most.

games.q: you're dancing in the circle at a wedding. a man stands off to the side with a heavy face. in Rebbe Nachman's picture, what does joy do?
o: leaves him alone until he feels better.
takes him by the hands and pulls him into the dance.
games.why: joy reaches over and pulls sadness into the circle. the sadness comes along, and begins to move.

practice: Let the corners of your mouth lift, even if it feels a little silly; Rebbe Nachman wouldn't mind silly.
Breathe in and think of one thing you're glad exists, breathe out and let a little heaviness go, and if something hard is sitting with you today, don't push it away: invite it into the circle.
If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words, I have set the LORD always before me.

wordCard.voice: Always joyful. Rebbe Nachman's teaching that being joyful always is a great mitzvah: joy as steady work, pulling sadness into the dance. Today's words.

orig.note: Hebrew: always, continually. Also the name of the daily Temple offering.

carryVoice: Your line: joy is a mitzvah, kept up on hard days. Joy, for Rebbe Nachman, is work you keep doing, not weather. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: I have set the LORD always before me
